candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Rewrite a nonstandard number form into a standard equivalent form before subtraction, such as converting a mixed number with an improper fractional part into a standard mixed number or simplifying a fraction part inside a mixed number.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A.S01, B.S01, and C.S01 all cover pre-subtraction normalization of nonstandard forms like improper mixed-number parts; C states this most cleanly. A and B also include rewriting a whole number as whole plus 0 over a denominator, but C separates that into a distinct skill, so only the overlapping normalization concept is aligned here.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Rewrite a whole number as a whole plus a zero fractional part using a needed denominator so it can be subtracted componentwise.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: C.S02 isolates the specific act of rewriting a whole number as a mixed or fractional form with 0 in the numerator. In A and B this action is bundled inside their broader normalization skills rather than separated, so there is no standalone equivalent skill to align from those codebooks.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Find a common denominator and convert fraction parts to equivalent fractions with that denominator before subtracting.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A.S02, B.S02, and C.S03 are direct matches in name and definition, all describing denominator alignment through equivalent-fraction conversion before subtraction.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Subtract fractional quantities once they are in compatible form, including subtracting numerators of like fractions or the fractional parts of mixed numbers.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A.S03 and B.S03 match closely as a fraction-only subtraction operation after denominators are compatible. C does not separate fraction-part subtraction from whole-part subtraction, instead combining them in C.S04.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Subtract the whole-number components of the quantities, including whole parts of mixed numbers or a whole number minus zero whole parts.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A.S04 and B.S04 are direct equivalents focused specifically on whole-part subtraction in mixed-number or whole-number contexts. C folds this operation into its broader componentwise subtraction skill C.S04.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Subtract quantities once they are in compatible form, including subtracting numerators of like fractions and subtracting whole parts and fraction parts separately in mixed-number problems.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: C.S04 is broader than either A or B's subtraction skills because it combines fraction-part subtraction and whole-part subtraction into one componentwise operation. Since A and B split this into separate skills, C.S04 is kept as its own aligned concept rather than forcing it into only one of those narrower categories.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Regroup one whole as fractional units and adjust the whole part when the fractional part is too small to subtract directly in a mixed-number or whole-minus-fraction problem.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A.S05, B.S05, and C.S05 are clear equivalents describing borrowing/regrouping from the whole part into fractional units when direct subtraction would produce a negative or insufficient fractional part.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Combine the computed whole and fractional parts into the final answer and reduce any fraction or zero-valued fraction to lowest terms or integer form.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A.S06, B.S06, and C.S06 all describe final-answer formation and simplification, including reducing fractions, collapsing zero fractional parts, and expressing the result in an appropriate final form.

alignment_summary: The three codebooks show strong agreement on denominator alignment, borrowing/regrouping, and final simplification/composition, with direct 3-way matches for those concepts. A and B also align closely in splitting subtraction into separate fraction-part and whole-part skills, while C instead combines those into one broader componentwise subtraction skill. C additionally separates rewriting a whole number as a whole plus 0 over a denominator from other normalization, whereas A and B include that action inside a broader normalization skill.
